And as an officer of this Court, of course, as you have long been, your commission as Attorney General will be duly recorded with the Clerk. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice. We'll hear arguments first this morning. In 78, 740, Angus, the Secretary of the Interior against Allard. Mr. Shapiro, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. This case is here on direct appeal by the government from an order of a three-judge district court in Colorado. The District Court entered a declaratory judgment and an injunction restraining the enforcement of two acts designed to protect our nation's birds, the Eagle Protection Act and the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. Those acts prohibit the sale of any parts of protected birds. The District Court decided that neither act applies to birds killed before the act prohibited the sale of the parts. That means that under the District Court's decision that items containing old feathers, that is, pre-prohibition feathers, can be sold. The Appellees have various commercial interests in things made by Indians. The Allards, the Bovases, and Ward own stores that trade in Indian items. Kelly works in the Bovis store, and Eros is an appraiser of Indian items. Some of these items are quite old and rare, and some are made in part of feathers. In response to interrogatories, the Appellees have identified about 40 such items they own and apparently wish to sell. The items contain the feathers of birds protected by either the Eagle Protection Act or the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, feathers that Appellees claim are pre-prohibition. Almost all of the feathers are eagle feathers. The Eagle Protection Act and the Migratory Bird Treaty Act both prohibit the sale of any parts of the birds to which they apply. They also, of course, prohibit hunting or killing those birds, or any commercial dealing in the birds themselves. We have discussed the Migratory Bird Treaty Act in our main brief and our reply brief in some detail. But the first point I want to emphasize today is that this is an Eagle Protection Act case far more than it is a Migratory Bird Treaty Act case. The question of whether the Eagle Act applies to old feathers is more important both to the government and to the Appellees than whether the Migratory Bird Treaty Act applies. And if you are correct about the Eagle Act, you win, don't you, without consideration of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act? Well, we win, assuming that the Appellees don't want to take the Eagle Feathers off of the items they own and sell them as... Well, if they wanted to take them off and took them off, they'd be exempt under the other act, wouldn't they? No. Wouldn't they? Because there are about seven artifacts, I think, that contain both Eagle Feathers and Migratory Bird Treaty Act feathers. I see. So as to those, they could take the Eagle Feathers off and then there would be a question of whether they could sell them, and that would turn on the applicability of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. Now that I've interrupted you, what do you say about the hypothetical case adverted to by your colleague on the other side, that the vendor or the seller could simply take all the feathers off these artifacts and sell the artifacts without feathers and then just make a gift of the feathers? Well, that we think would certainly be a violation. It would be an evasion of the Act. The Act prohibits the sale, exchange or barter of the feathers. But not gifts. Not gifts. And if the... I mean, if it was part of the same sales transaction, merely separating the artifact wouldn't make it a different sales transaction. It would be a matter of litigating the facts. It certainly would. That's the ultimate question, is that the trier of fact would have to decide whether this was a sale of feathers that was... or a barter exchange that was within the prohibitions of the statute. Mrs. Shapiro, the Court did not reach the constitutional question, did it? No, it decided the case on statutory grounds. It stated that the reason it was deciding it on statutory grounds was in part to avoid serious constitutional questions. What was the occasion then for continuing the three-judge courts? Well, we argued in our jurisdictional statement that, in fact, the three-judge court was not necessary because the constitutional questions were not substantial. Well, then, should this case not have gone to the Court of Appeals? That was the argument that we made in the jurisdictional statement. The difficulty was that the appeal to the Court of Appeals was filed one day late, and we thought... But haven't we, on some occasions, corrected the... the putative three-judge court to enter a new judgment under the law and appeal to the Court of Appeals? Yes. And... Do you think that would be an appropriate solution here? Yes, that's the solution we urge this Court to adopt in the jurisdictional statement, yes. But despite your urging, we know the problem is your statement. That's right, yes. It isn't too late to follow that force now. No, it's not. On your submission that the constitutional issue is frivolous? Yes. Despite the three judges thinking to the contrary? That's right. The reason this case is that the EGLE Protection Act is more important to this case for the appellees is because of the the fact that almost all the items that they have identified contain eagle feathers. Almost none contain Migratory Bird Treaty Act feathers. The EGLE Act is more important to the government in this context because the appellees' artifacts are typical. The question involved here is more likely to arise in the enforcement of the EGLE Act than of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. The question comes up mostly in connection with Indian items, and the feathers in those items are usually eagle feathers. I emphasize this point because the district court focused on the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, and appellees repeat that error. They thus avoid facing both the plain language of the EGLE Act and the justification for that language, Congress's desire to protect our national symbol from extinction. I turn now to those two points. The EGLE Protection Act was enacted in 1940 in order to protect the bald eagle. It was extended to the Golden Eagle in 1962. The act prohibits the killing or taking of eagles. It also prohibits the possession, sale, or purchase of eagle parts. There are only a few carefully limited exceptions to this total ban. The most important for this case is an exception that permits the possession and transportation of the parts of eagles taken before the act applied to them. That is, the act says that no one may possess, purchase, or sell eagle parts, except that pre-prohibition eagle parts may be possessed. We submit that the negative implication is absolutely clear. No one may purchase or sell pre-prohibition eagle parts. This is not a case where you have to decide what Congress would have done if they had focused on a problem. Congress did focus on the problem of pre-prohibition parts and decided that they could be possessed, but not purchased or sold. The total ban on any sale of eagle feathers, including pre-prohibition feathers, is an important part of the legislative plan for protecting the living eagle population. There are three related factors that justify the ban. First, there is the difficulty in distinguishing between old and new feathers. There is no scientifically reliable way of proving how old a feather is, and certainly not of whether it comes from an eagle killed before 1940. Second, there is the high value of feathered Indian artifacts. Apelle Ward has a ceremonial shield that he claims is worth $7,500. And the other apellees have identified twelve other items that they have valued at more than $1,000 each. Third, there is the very real possibility that the bald eagle, our national symbol, may come extinct in this country outside of Alaska. That was the reason Congress passed the act in 1940, the reason it extended it to the golden eagle in 1962. The problem apparently is that golden eagles and bald eagles can't be told apart before they reach maturity. And the reason that Congress strengthened the act in 1972. The possibility of extinction still exists today. A recent survey indicates that there are fewer than 800 eagle nests in the original 48 states. The value of old feathered artifacts, plus the ease of passing off new feathers for old, taken together, give a strong incentive to counterfeit artifacts for sale, or at least to replace lost feathers in genuine artifacts that are offered for sale. Eagles will be killed to supply the necessary feathers. And a total ban on sales destroys the market and saves those eagles. Even if a relatively few eagles are saved this way, those few may be important to the survival of species in the original 48 states. Congress could have decided that less drastic methods would be good enough. It could have struck a different balance between the importance of saving the eagle and the interest of dealers in Indian artifacts. But the point is that any less drastic measure, for instance the registration system that the district court thought would be sufficient, would provide less protection to the eagle. If there's any market for old feathered artifacts, they're so valuable that they're likely to be counterfeited. A counterfeiter who believes he can persuade a purchaser that the feathers in his article are old is also likely that he can persuade a registrar, and ultimately a judge or a jury of that fact. For that reason, the most effective deterrent to counterfeiting, and to the eagle killing it requires, is to abolish the market by a total ban on any sale of feathers. And that's the solution that Congress chose. That choice violated no constitutional right of appellees. The violation they claim is a taking of their property without just compensation. As we explain in our brief, appellees have no standing to raise this constitutional claim with regard to either act, because they have not alleged that they themselves owned any of these feathers when the act first applied to them. Was that argument made in the district court? The standing argument? No, but it's a jurisdictional argument. Unless they did. The act couldn't have taken anything from them. What do you mean by standing? Whether they're standing to raise a... Well, what do you mean by standing? Whether they have the right to raise this argument. No, but the argument is that whether or whenever we own this, whether you agree with the argument or not is another matter. The argument is that it doesn't make any difference. Whenever they have fired it, there is a statutory issue. Oh, yes. I'm sorry. I didn't understand. We don't have any... Well, it isn't a jurisdictional issue. It's... We don't contend that they don't have standing to raise the statutory issue. Mm-hmm. But we do contend they don't have standing to raise the constitutional issue. I know, but the constitutional argument is the same. They still assert that whenever we acquire this, there is a constitutional issue here. But... Now, you may not agree with it, and you may think it's a worse argument than if they had acquired it before, the act. But the argument is there. Well, the... But... It's there in the sense that... Well, if it is, they certainly have standing to raise that issue, don't they? Well, I have standing to make the argument that their property... They have standing to argue that even if we acquired the feathers after the relevant acts were passed, the statute is unconstitutional and is applied to us. Well, they have standing to make that argument. Surely, they have standing to do it. But you may not... You may think the argument is... There's even less to it than the constitutional issue with respect to feathers that were acquired prior to the act. But they certainly can assert it. Well, I assume they're attacking both of them. No, they're rather careful to say that they... No, no, not post-act feathers, but they're attacking the application to pre-act feathers that were acquired by them post-act. That's the... That's what you say they don't have the standards you raise. Yes, yes. I'm just suggesting to you that they do. Well, that's... You say it's characteristic, but I just suggest it. Well, in any event, the act... As to feathers that they acquired after the act became effective, the act itself took nothing that they had. What it did was prevent them from obtaining something when they acquired the feathers after the act became effective. Mr. Shapiro, we've got you interrupted, and I'd like to ask one other question, if I may. You mentioned the figures on the number of eagle nests in the 48 states. What is the relevance of the eagle population in Alaska, and what is it? Well, the eagle population in Alaska is somewhat larger than it is in the lower 48 states. I'm sorry, I don't have the figures for the numbers. If there's no shortage of eagles in Alaska, is your necessity argument valid? Isn't this a nationwide statute, not just 48 states? Well, it certainly is a reasonable conclusion for Congress that the eagle deserves very strict protection. The fact that there are somewhat more eagles in Alaska doesn't alter the fact that the eagle is in a rather parlous situation, and that Congress was perfectly reasonable in concluding that a very strict law was appropriate. So you don't rest on the fact that there... I mean, the eagle population really isn't terribly relevant to your argument. It's relevant to the extent that Congress was legitimately concerned about preserving eagles. In 48 states? In 48 states. And killing in Alaska is also... interferes with the population up there, and it's not... they're not limitless. Mr. Shapiro, this is an inconsequential question, but I'm curious. The Eagle Act was passed in 1940, and the regulations came along in 63, 23 years later, right? No. The Eagle Act was passed in 1940. The first regulations were in 1941. I believe we discussed in footnote 7 of our main brief. When did the regulations come out under the other act? The Migratory Bird Treaty Act? Well, I'm sure there have been regulations of some kind, very... since shortly after the act was enacted. I didn't get that impression in the brief, but then you may be right. The... The... The regulations have been certainly expanded and modified as new birds are added to the Migratory Bird Treaty Act. But it's not a question of their not having been there. For instance... If there were delays, I'd be interested in why, but you say there hasn't been to them. There certainly has been no delay under the Eagle Act. And the regulations under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act originally were fairly minor. The Migratory Bird Treaty Act is primarily a hunting act. And it was... The regulations were modified in early 1973 to make absolutely explicit the Secretary's interpretation of the Act as applying to pre-prohibition feathers. Before that, they were arguably ambiguous. But there certainly have been regulations. Well, they're in the... I don't see how you can... The court of regulations in 68. How can you say they're arguably ambiguous when they almost parroted the language of the statute, which you said was abundantly clear? Well, on the theory that regulations ordinarily are more specific... Do you think the statutory prohibition in the Eagle Statute would be clear if there were not the proviso in the statute? Well, I think it would. It would. It would be less clear. I mean... It would be clear if it applied to pre-act Eagles even without the proviso there. The thing is, as we've mentioned, that in the Eagle Act, Congress did specifically focus on this question in so many words. Do you have evidence of that other than the statutory language itself? I should think the potential language would be enough. Well, I mean, that is what you're talking about. That is what I'm talking about, yes. And there's no... There's no evidence of any discussion in committee about the problem of pre-act Eagles. No, no. There's really very little legislative history. There's... I guess we pointed out in our reply brief that in the 62 Act they did mention their concern with Indian... killing of Indian Eagles in the Sculling... No, they said there's nothing wrong with the barter, as I read, as I read. There's nothing wrong with bartering, Indians exchanging Eagle feathers, which would seem to have been explicitly prohibited by the statute under your reading. Well, the legislative history didn't... What the legislative history was saying was that the main problem for Eagles, the motivation for killing the Eagles, was to sell them to dealers in artifacts and... But didn't the committee also say we can't see anything wrong with Indians exchanging feathers for religious purposes in the line? Well, that's quite a different situation. The exchange of feathers for religious purposes is only under specific permits issued by the Secretary on the... in the... and before issuing them, he issues them Indian by Indian for a very limited period, and only after he has made the determination that that won't interfere with the survival of the population. So it's a very narrow limitation. Without those specific exceptions, that would have been prohibited by the statute. Oh, yes. Yes. And the religious purposes is in the statute. We also pointed out in our briefs that under the Regional Rail Reorganization Act cases, the remedy of anyone who does have standing is a suit in the Court of Claims under the Tucker Act for just compensation. We do not suggest that anyone could prevail in such a suit, because we do not think these acts under any circumstances involve a taking in the constitutional sense. But even if we are wrong about the merits, and these acts could in some factual circumstances involve taking a property requiring just compensation, those circumstances have not been shown here. This record just does not provide an adequate basis for deciding the novel and complex issues that would have to be faced before a court could properly conclude that there had been a taking here. For example, Apelle's claim is that the acts place such a heavy burden on them that fairness and justice require that they receive compensation. The burden they identify is the total loss of value of their artifacts containing pre-prohibition feathers. But Apelle's claim is that the artifacts can be sold without the feathers. That is true. Anyone who is more interested in making money than in the integrity of his artifacts is free under either act to remove the feathers and sell the rest. That sale does not threaten the living bird population. And that sale is not prohibited by the act. As I mentioned before, we do not agree with the Apelle's suggestion that the ban can be avoided either by separating the feathers and attempting to make them a separate transaction. Or, of course, that the article can be sold intact and just claim that it was a sale of the artifact without the feathers and a gift of the attached feathers. But it is still true that the acts prohibit only the sale of feathers and of products composed of feathers. Apelle Ward, for instance, could remove the nine eagle feathers from his ceremonial shield and sell it without violating the act. There is no way of telling from this record what the value of the shield would be in that condition. But any burden on Ward is limited to the difference between the value of the shield with the feathers and its value without them. Discounted, probably, by his right to retain possession of the shield intact if he chooses to do so. Since the record doesn't show how much the value of any artifact would be reduced if its feathers were removed, there is no way of telling what burden the act places on any apelle, let alone of concluding that the burden is one which, in fairness and justice, must be shared by the public. But there is no need for this court to advance into that figure. Apellees have simply not met their burden of showing that the acts take their property without just compensation. Unless there are any further questions, I would like to reserve the remainder of my time. Very well, Mrs. Shapiro. Mr. Eichholz. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. The Appellant's argument has solely addressed itself to the preservation of existing wildlife. In this particular action, however, we are not concerned with wildlife alone, but with antiquities, feathered Indian artifacts for which there is also an express federal policy of encouraging private preservation. The Historic Sites and Antiquities Act, 16 U.S. Code Section 470, specifically recognizes that cultural objects such as are before the court, have been predominantly preserved by private efforts, and states that it is the federal policy to provide for the maximum encouragement of the continued preservation of such items by private means. Whatever else might be said of the regulations, by essentially having made it unlawful to continue with the ability to preserve such artifacts by private means, and certainly contrary to the express policy of the historic sites and antiquities act. This action is specifically concerned with 42 pre-act feathered Indian artifacts. They stand admitted in the record as being pre-act, and additionally they stand admitted as being valueless if they are unable to be sold with the feathers intact. The action in the District Court was on a cross motion for summary judgment, and no issue was raised in the court as to the pre-existing nature of the feathers, nor was any issue made in the trial court that the artifacts themselves would have any value whatever if the feathers had to be removed and sold without the feathers, which are an integral part of most feathered Indian artifacts. Mr. A. Colt, does the record show when your clients obtained these artifacts, before or after the acts? Mr. A. Colt, does the record show when your clients obtained these artifacts? Mr. A. Colt, in large part, your honor, the answers of the appellees to the interrogatories submitted by the Secretary does state the years in which these items were acquired. Mr. A. Colt, were those years that you stated before or after the passage of the relevant acts? Mr. A. Colt, they were after the passage of the acts. In the history of the acts, as Mr. Shapiro has noted, the Eagle Protection Act originally was enacted in 1940. They were all acquired after 1940. Additionally, they were all acquired after 1962 with respect to Eagle Feathers. Mr. A. Colt, was any issue raised about the standing of your clients in the district court? Mr. A. Colt, not as to that issue on standing, your honor, in the trial court. The issue was whether or not there was a case or controversy upon the basis that there was a lack of any administrative enforcement. Mr. A. Colt, well, the district court apparently approached the case on the basis that even if your clients did acquire these artifacts, after the passage of the acts, the relevant acts just didn't apply to them. Mr. A. Colt, that is correct, your honor. Mr. A. Colt, that was your position? Mr. A. Colt, that was our position as well. And it was irrelevant when a certain party acquired those pre-existing artifacts. That is correct, Your Honor. So long as the objects themselves were pre-act artifacts. That is correct. The premise of the Solicitor General's Office is that these items must be totally banned from commerce upon the basis that there is an existing market for counterfeit items which must be supplied by the taking of birds, of existing birds from the wild. These premises are not supported by the record, and their position is an impermissible attempt in which to infer a negative from an omission in the statutes, or more particularly, to infer a negative from the positive statement, none of which can be statutorily sustained. Mr. Ackle, don't they start with the plain language argument, and then they say this is the reason for the plain language, and how do you meet their plain language argument that the coverage of the Act is broad on barter, sale, and so forth, and the only exception with respect to pre-act items are possession and transportation? Yes, Your Honor. How do you meet that argument? The Acts themselves do not specifically include pre-act items. They are concerned with birds and parts of birds, whereas this Court and the issue concerned with this Court is something in addition to birds and parts thereof. The Migratory Bird Treaty Act alone also includes the term products, which products I will address shortly. Mr. Justice Holmes in McBoyle v. United States 283, United States 25, was concerned with whether or not the term motor vehicle included a boat or an airplane, and he said, in common terms, it called to mind a picture of a thing moving across the land, an automobile. The same determination can be applied to the use of the terms birds and bird parts in these statutes. In common terms, such partial terminology does not include pre-existing Indian artifacts any more than it would make logical sense to call them wood or cloth or any of their other component terms. Except maybe your argument would be valid if there were not the proviso. That's what makes it, that seems to me that's what lends a lot of force to their argument. It does not address, and is not designed to address, the Fifth Amendment question because it is our position and understanding that the Eagle Protection Act itself does not apply to pre-existing artifacts. The sole matter raised by the appellate... The proviso does. The proviso does in words. The proviso in so many words talks about pre-existing items. And why doesn't, given the proviso, why doesn't the previous part necessarily apply to pre-act parts, which parts would include others, of course? Because we do not believe that simply by the use of the term parts, the legislature was considering pre-act Indian artifacts among other types of materials. What you're saying is the proviso really was not necessary. It was just thrown in as kind of an abundance of caution. I think it is necessary, Your Honor, to avoid an obviously invalid ex post facto act. Because if they made possession alone illegal, the entire act must fall because without any further affirmative act by an owner of such items... But I think you're contradicting yourself because if I understood you correctly, you were saying without the proviso, the first part of the statute simply doesn't apply to pre-act items. So it just wouldn't apply. There wouldn't be violate the ex post facto clause or anything else. It simply wouldn't apply.
